classification_signals: The article synthesizes empirical evidence from psychological research (p. 1, abstract). It discusses and applies existing theories like McAndrew and Koehnke's (2016) theory of creepiness (p. 1, abstract, p. 4), Appleton's Prospect-Refuge theory (p. 2), and agent detection mechanisms (p. 4-5). It cites numerous empirical studies throughout the text to support its claims (e.g., Kaplan 1987, Fisher and Nasar 1992, Watt et al. 2017). The paper does not present new empirical data from the authors.
title: The Psychology, Geography, and Architecture of Horror: How Places Creep Us Out

minimum_safe_summary: The paper explores why certain places evoke feelings of creepiness and horror, proposing that these responses stem from evolved psychological mechanisms designed to detect potential threats in ambiguous situations. It synthesizes empirical evidence from environmental, evolutionary, and cognitive psychology, applying theories such as Prospect-Refuge, agent detection, and threat ambiguity to explain how architectural features, social isolation, associations with death or tragic events, and sensory cues like infrasound contribute to feelings of dread. The paper argues that horror entertainment taps into these same mechanisms, allowing for safe mental rehearsal of threat responses, and highlights how top-down processing and existing beliefs can perpetuate perceptions of haunted places. The paper does not explicitly state its own limitations.

paper_metadata.title: The Psychology, Geography, and Architecture of Horror: How Places Creep Us Out
paper_metadata.crossref_title: The Psychology, Geography, and Architecture of Horror: How Places Creep Us Out
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: AbstractWhy do some types of settings and some combinations of sensory information induce a sense of dread in humans? This article brings empirical evidence from psychological research to bear on the experience of horror, and explains why the tried-and-true horror devices intuitively employed by writers and filmmakers work so well. Natural selection has favored individuals who gravitated toward environments containing the “right” physical and psychological features and avoided those which posed a threat. Places that contain a bad mix of these features induce unpleasant feelings of dread and fear, and therefore have become important ingredients of the settings for horror fiction and films. This article ap­plies McAndrew and Koehnke’s (2016) theory of creepiness to the study of classic horror settings and explores the role played by architecture, isolation, association with death, and other environmental qualities in the experience of creepiness and dread.
